title: Garland, Wreaths and Bows: Front Entrance Decorating Ideas
metaTitle: Garland, Wreaths and Bows: Entrance Ideas
metaDescription: Lights are only part of a great front entrance. Here are garland, wreath and bow ideas Waterloo Region homeowners use to finish their Christmas display.
excerpt: A roofline full of lights sets the tone, but the front entrance is what visitors actually walk up to. Here is how garland, wreaths and bows pull a Waterloo Region display together.

body.text: A house with a beautifully lit roofline but a bare front door looks unfinished up close, even if it looks impressive from the street. The front entrance is the one part of a Christmas display that guests, delivery drivers and trick-or-treaters' parents dropping off cookies all experience at arm's length rather than from a car window, and it deserves the same design attention as the roofline itself. Garland, wreaths and bows are what typically fill that gap, and getting the proportions, placement and colour coordination right is what separates an entrance that looks pulled together from one that looks like an afterthought.
Start with the wreath, not the lights

It is tempting to plan a display roofline-first and treat the front door as an afterthought, but the wreath is usually the single most noticed decorative element on a home, precisely because it sits at eye level right where people approach the house. The most common mistake is proportion: a wreath that is too small for a large door with substantial trim looks lost, while an oversized wreath on a narrower door or one with sidelights can overwhelm the entrance and interfere with the door swinging open comfortably.

A general rule that works well for most Waterloo Region homes is to size the wreath to roughly a third to a half of the door's width, adjusted for how much surrounding trim or glass is on the door itself. Full-glass doors or doors with sidelights typically look best with a wreath sized to sit clearly within the solid portion of the door, rather than one large enough to partially cover the glass. Homes with double doors sometimes work better with two matching, smaller wreaths rather than one oversized centre piece, which also creates a nice symmetry when viewed from the front walk.
Layering garland for depth

Garland draped along a railing, across a porch beam, or framing a doorway adds a texture and depth that lights alone cannot achieve. The most effective approach is layering: a base run of fresh or high-quality faux evergreen garland, with a secondary layer of small lights woven through it, and then accent pieces like pinecones, berries or ribbon tucked in at intervals rather than spread perfectly evenly. Evenly spaced accents tend to look mechanical up close, while slightly varied spacing reads as more natural, which is generally the effect homeowners are after with evergreen decor.

Porch railings are one of the most common and most effective places for garland in Waterloo Region, since most homes in Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge and Guelph have some kind of railed porch, step or entrance structure to work with. Garland draped along the top rail, with the ends anchored securely at the newel posts, creates a strong visual frame for the entrance without competing with the wreath on the door itself. For homes with a portico or overhang, garland can also run along the header above the door, which draws the eye upward and ties the entrance into the roofline lighting above it.
Where bows actually help

Bows are best treated as an accent rather than a centrepiece. A well-placed bow at the top of a wreath, at intervals along a garland run, or anchoring the ends of a garland swag on a railing pulls a colour scheme together without adding visual clutter. The most common misstep is using too many bows or bows that are too large relative to the wreath or garland they are attached to, which ends up drawing attention to the bow itself rather than reinforcing the overall look.

Colour coordination between the bow, the lights, and any coloured accents elsewhere in the display matters more than most homeowners initially expect. A home with warm white lights and a natural evergreen colour palette generally pairs well with deep red, burgundy or gold bows, while a home leaning into a more traditional multicolour light scheme has more flexibility to introduce brighter reds, greens or even plaid patterns without clashing. The goal is for the bow to feel like it belongs to the same design decision as the lights, not like a separate purchase added on afterward.

The most cohesive entrances are the ones where the wreath, garland, bows and lights were planned together as one design rather than assembled piece by piece. A single conversation with our team covers all of it at once.
Matching the entrance to the rest of the display

An entrance that is decorated in isolation from the rest of the house's lighting scheme often looks like two separate projects rather than one cohesive display. If the roofline is done in warm white LED, extending that same warm white into the garland lighting keeps the whole house reading as one consistent design when viewed from the street. Similarly, if trees on the property are being wrapped as part of a tree lighting package, coordinating the colour and density of those wraps with the entrance decor creates a display that feels intentional from every angle, not just the one most visible from the road. More detail on how tree wraps are typically approached is available at /services/tree-lighting-services.

This is one of the advantages of having a single company handle design and installation for the entire property rather than piecing together lights from one source and greenery from another. Classic Christmas Lighting's full decoration service, covered in more detail at /services/christmas-decoration-services, is built around exactly this kind of coordinated approach, treating the entrance, the roofline and any tree lighting as one design rather than three separate decisions.
Durability matters more than it looks like it should

Southern Ontario winters are hard on outdoor decor. Wind, freeze-thaw cycles, and the occasional heavy wet snowfall all put real stress on anything mounted outdoors for two to three months. A wreath hung with a simple nail or hook can end up crooked or on the ground after the first significant windstorm, and garland that is not properly secured at multiple points along its length tends to sag in the middle within a few weeks, which undercuts the polished look it started with. Professional installation addresses this with secure mounting designed to hold through the season, not just look good on the day it goes up.

There is also the question of what happens to doors, railings and trim after the season ends. Improperly mounted decor, especially anything attached with adhesive hooks, nails, or wire wrapped directly around painted trim, can leave marks, scuffs or small areas of damage once removed. Professional installation and removal are designed specifically to avoid this, which matters for homeowners who want their entrance looking as good in January, after everything comes down, as it did before the season started.
Ideas by entrance style

Different entrance styles in Waterloo Region tend to suit slightly different approaches. A classic centre-hall home with a single prominent front door and modest portico generally looks best with a single well-proportioned wreath, garland framing the door itself rather than a full railing run, and a single coordinated bow at the top of the wreath. A wider farmhouse-style porch with a full railing benefits from the layered garland-along-the-railing approach described earlier, with the wreath as a secondary focal point rather than the sole feature. Homes with a covered porch and pillars can extend garland up the pillars themselves, wrapped in a spiral with small lights woven through, which adds vertical interest that a flat door display alone cannot achieve.

For businesses in Guelph, Cambridge or elsewhere in the region looking to apply similar entrance decorating to a storefront, the same principles of proportion, layering and colour coordination apply, just scaled to a commercial entrance and often paired with a broader Christmas lighting for businesses package. A commercial entrance often benefits from slightly bolder, larger-scale garland and wreaths than a residential door, since storefronts are typically viewed from a greater distance by passing foot and vehicle traffic.

faq.q: What size wreath should I use for my front door?
faq.a: A good general guideline is sizing the wreath to roughly a third to a half of the door's width, adjusted for trim and any glass panels. Doors with sidelights or full glass generally look best with a wreath sized to sit within the solid portion of the door.

faq.q: Should garland lights match the roofline lights?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. Matching the colour temperature, such as warm white to warm white, between garland and roofline lighting keeps the whole display reading as one cohesive design rather than two separate projects.

faq.q: How many bows should an entrance display have?
faq.a: Fewer, well-placed bows generally look better than several scattered ones. A single bow at the top of a wreath or bows anchoring the ends of a garland swag are usually enough to tie the colour scheme together without adding clutter.

faq.q: Will garland or wreaths damage my door or railings?
faq.a: Improperly mounted decor, especially adhesive hooks or wire wrapped directly around trim, can leave marks. Professional installation uses secure mounting designed to avoid damage and comes down cleanly after the season.

faq.q: Can entrance decor be added to an existing lighting installation?
faq.a: Yes. Garland, wreaths and bows can be added as part of a new installation or layered onto an existing Christmas light display to round out the overall look.

faq.q: Does the decoration service work for commercial entrances too?
faq.a: Yes. The same design principles apply to storefronts and commercial entrances, generally scaled up in size since they are viewed from a greater distance than a residential doorway.
